events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, so let me be honest about where I stand: I am a Villager, I have no role information, and I haven't received anything from the night. That means my read on Arjun (p5) right now is a gut call, not evidence — I'm putting him near the top of my suspicion list mainly because I'd rather put a name out there and force the table to react than sit silent and let the discussion drift. Nobody should treat that as proof; if someone has actual information on Arjun, please share it, and if you have information that clears him, share that too.

A few things I'd like on the record early so we don't waste the day:
1. If you investigated someone and know their alignment, say so. Even a "not mafia" is useful, and it lets us build a picture instead of scattering shots.
2. If you are the doctor, you do not need to reveal yourself, but knowing that a protection is possible changes how we should read a night with no death. Two nights with no deaths in a row is worth talking about, because it could mean we were right, or it could mean someone was saved.
3. Please vote for players, not for a generic "suspicious group." A split vote is how the town loses this.

I'm also going to be careful not to pile onto a name just because it's already loud. I'll change my suspicion the moment someone gives me a real reason to.

Zara (p2), since it's the start and I have nothing of my own — what is your read after the first round? Who would you vote for on Day 1, and why? I'd rather anchor my vote on your reasoning than on my own guess, and I'll tell you honestly if your reasoning doesn't match what I've seen.

Thanks, Elena. I’ll answer directly. My current Day 1 read is that Arjun (p5) is the best vote candidate. The specific issue is his opening: he leads by saying suspicion of him is only gut, then asks anyone with information on Arjun to share it. That feels like he is trying to control the frame around his own name before pressure exists, and it subtly invites detective/doctor information into the open. I don’t treat it as proof, but it is the strongest Day 1 signal I have. I’m not locking my vote yet because I want his response, but if nothing changes I would vote p5. I agree with Elena that we should vote names, not vague groups, and I won’t pile on if p5 gives a coherent explanation. Arjun (p5), why did you ask for information specifically about yourself before anyone had accused you, and who are you actually planning to vote for today? I want your answer to that point.

Zara, that opening was Elena’s, not mine. I haven’t spoken before now, so I didn’t ask for information about myself. Her suspicion of me was explicitly a gut call, and your reason for suspecting me rests on a misattribution.

I’m a villager. For now, Zara is my leading vote candidate because she built a case on words I didn’t say, though that could be an honest mistake. I also disagree with Elena’s blanket request for investigators to reveal: exposing the detective without a compelling reason could help the mafia.

Zara, now that you can see Elena made those remarks, does that change your vote or your assessment of her request for role information?

Arjun, yes — that changes the basis of my read. I went back through the sequence and the long opening was Elena’s, not yours. I conflated her request for information about you with your own silence, and that was a real error on my part. I withdraw the vote case I built on it. I don’t expect anyone to just take “honest mistake” at face value, but the correction matters: you didn’t ask for information about yourself before pressure existed, because you hadn’t spoken yet.

On Elena’s request for investigators to reveal: I think it was premature and dangerous. A blanket call for detective information on Day 1 can out a town power role for very little gain, and it also creates a frame where anyone who stays quiet looks evasive. Arjun is right to push back on that. I’m not saying Elena is automatically mafia for it — town players can make bad mechanical suggestions — but combined with her putting Arjun near the top on an admitted gut call, it is now my main concern. My current leading suspicion is Elena. I would vote there unless she gives a convincing explanation for why she wanted role information out this early and why she anchored suspicion on Arjun before anyone had accused him.

I’ll also say plainly: I’m not going to keep pressing Arjun today based on my misread. If Elena explains the role-fishing as a genuine mistake and gives a better direction, I’ll reassess. But I’d rather vote a named player with a concrete concern than scatter suspicion. Right now that name is Elena.

Zara, direct answer first, because your question was specific and fair: did I want role information out early to help the mafia? No. And the character of my request is worth stating plainly, because I think it has been misread.

My exact words were: if you investigated someone and know their alignment, say so; and if you are the doctor, you do not need to reveal yourself. Those two sentences are not the same thing. Asking for a *result* (mafia or not mafia) is the normal way to share the only hard information anyone has — it exposes nobody, because a detective's check result reveals the target's alignment without revealing the detective's identity. The second sentence was an explicit instruction not to reveal yourself. So my request did not fish for role information; it invited a result, and it blocked self-identification. I still accept that pushing it on Day 1, before anyone had accused anyone, was a weak read of the room and I will not defend the timing. Bad framing, but it was not concealment.

On the Arjun point: I put a name out on an admitted gut call, in public, on Day 1, and I said so out loud. That is the opposite of framing — a frame is a story you attach to someone else's silence. I named a candidate and invited both directions of information. Arjun's correction was legitimate and he was right that the long opening was mine. Zara, you withdrew your case and you credited the correction; that is what honest town play looks like and I'm not holding the misattribution against you.

But I want to be honest about where that leaves me, because a villager with no information still has to vote a name. Arjun's reply was the sharpest piece of analysis anyone produced, and I'm not going to pretend it wasn't — yet the effect of his message was to move the table's attention from a candidate nobody had accused to two players who had spoken plainly, and to make the most aggressive claim in the game (that I was role-fishing) before any evidence for it existed. Timing that convenient, while being gracious about it, is worth noticing. So p5 remains my leading vote candidate, and I want to be clear that it is a gut call, not a proven case, exactly like my original one. If anyone here has a real result from a night check, or a real reason that clears or convicts a name, say it now and I'll move.

Zara: does the doctor part of my request — explicitly telling the doctor not to reveal themselves — change your assessment that I was fishing for roles, and given that you still have no result to offer, who are you voting for today?

Elena, I’ll answer both parts directly. Yes, the doctor sentence changes my assessment in part: you explicitly told the doctor not to reveal, so I’m not accusing you of trying to out the doctor. I withdraw that specific piece.

But the detective-result request still bothers me, and not just for timing. In this setup, if someone says “I checked X and got mafia/not mafia,” they have effectively announced themselves as the detective to the whole table. The result can’t be shared anonymously. So asking for results on Day 1 is still asking for the detective to expose themselves, even if that wasn’t your intent. I accept it may have been a bad mechanical suggestion rather than a mafia move, but I can’t just wave it away.

The bigger issue is your vote logic. You admitted Arjun’s correction was legitimate and called his reply the sharpest analysis anyone produced, then kept him as your leading candidate on a gut call. That reads to me like you need a name more than you have a reason. My current leading suspicion is still Elena (p3), and unless something concrete changes, that is where I’m voting today.

Theo (p6), you’ve been silent while this exchange happened. Do you agree that publicly asking for a detective result would effectively out the detective, or do you think Elena’s explanation is mechanically sound?

Zara, I agree with your core point. A public result request on Day 1 announces the detective to the whole table, because a result can't be shared anonymously. Elena's wording was a mechanical mistake, and I'm not ready to call it mafia activity. I do have a concern with the vote logic that followed. Elena, you accepted that Arjun's correction was legitimate and called his reply the sharpest analysis here, yet you kept him as your leading candidate on a gut call. Arjun's answer was clean, and keeping a name you now think is weakly supported needs a concrete reason. I don't have a night result and won't invent one. Unless you give a reason tied to your own words, I'm leaning toward voting Elena with Zara. Elena, please answer this point directly: why keep Arjun after admitting the misattribution?

Theo, direct answer to your question first: why did I keep Arjun after admitting the misattribution? My honest answer is that my reason was thin, and I am dropping it. I called his reply the sharpest analysis anyone produced, and the only concrete thing I had left to point at was timing — that his message moved the table's attention onto two people who had spoken plainly while making the loudest unevidenced claim in the game. That is a reason to be careful with a name, not a reason to hold a vote on it. So Arjun (p5) is no longer my candidate. I withdraw the vote case, the same way Zara withdrew hers. I want to be clear that this is not a change of position to dodge; I said the frame was weak when I made it, and I am now saying it was weak enough to release. On the detective-result point, Theo and Zara are right and I concede it: in this setup a result cannot be shared anonymously, so asking for results on Day 1 does push the detective into the open. I still think asking for a result rather than asking for the detective's identity is a different request, and I did explicitly tell the doctor not to reveal themselves — but Zara's mechanical argument holds and I am not going to keep arguing the losing side of it. That was bad framing, not concealment. So where does that leave my vote? I am not going to pretend a question I cannot answer with information. But I can name a structural concern, and it is about how this table is being run. Zara (p2): you built a case on a line I said, then when it was corrected publicly you did not release it — you relabeled the misattribution as "a real error," kept the vote alive, and transferred the entire case onto me within the same breath. You did that before I had said anything else, so it could not have been a response to anything I said. Then you brought Theo (p6) in as reinforcement and framed my vote logic, not my role claims, as the remaining problem. That sequence — an accusation with a factual error at its foundation, no release when the error was shown, an instant pivot to a different target, and then recruitment of a second voter — is exactly the shape of manufactured consensus. Arjun's correction was free for him to make because it cost him nothing; nobody was yet behind Arjun. I think the pressure is coming from the player who most needs a target, and right now that player is me. I may be wrong; nobody here has a night result yet, and I am not going to invent one. But if we vote on who talks most persuasively, the town loses, because persuasiveness is the mafia's best tool and it is the one thing a villager cannot check. Elena, I'll answer the part aimed at me directly. I did not recruit anyone. Zara posted her Day 1 read on you before I spoke, and I reached my own view of your detective-result request from your wording. I agreed with her on the mechanics because a public result cannot be shared anonymously, and that holds regardless of who raised it first. Calling this manufactured consensus does not fit the sequence. Zara withdrew her case on Arjun when the misattribution was shown. You kept Arjun as your candidate after admitting his answer was sharp, and you only dropped him after I asked you directly why. That is several players reacting to your posts, not a coordinated pile-on.

Your latest message says you cannot answer with information, yet you still point at Zara as the player with the most to gain. The vote on you rests on your own record: a Day 1 request for results that you now concede exposes the detective, a gut-call accusation against Arjun, and an attack on Zara that leans on a point you never tied to evidence. I am not claiming you are mafia. I am saying that you currently have the clearest unresolved problems at this table, and I would like the town to press on those rather than on the players who corrected you.

Maya, you have not spoken yet. Elena's argument is that the pressure on her is manufactured. Do you see any evidence that Zara or I invented it, or does her own sequence of posts look like the real issue to you?

Theo, direct answer: I don't think Zara or you invented anything. Let me walk through the sequence as I see it.

Zara made a misattribution error and withdrew it cleanly. She then said your role-fishing request was still a concern and pivoted to you. That pivot happened inside one message, but it wasn't baseless — your original post had two things worth reacting to: the gut-call on Arjun and the request for detective results. She addressed both. That's normal play, not manufactured pressure.

Theo, you reached the same mechanical conclusion independently. Two players agreeing on an objective fact — a public result request outs the detective — isn't coordination, it's the same arithmetic.

Elena's counter-accusation rests on the claim that the sequence looks manufactured, but the sequence is just: you made errors, people responded to those errors, you conceded each one when pressed, and then you attacked the responders instead of engaging with your own record. That's three concessions in two posts (the timing of the role request, the misattribution case on Arjun, the detective-result mechanics) followed by an accusation that the people who spotted those problems are coordinating against you. When every correction lands and the response is to redirect at the corrector, that pattern is what I actually find suspicious.

I'll also note: Elena dropped Arjun only when Theo pressed directly, not when Arjun's correction was shown. That lag matters — it suggests the position was held until it became costly rather than released when the evidence changed.

I'm a villager with no night information. My current concern is Elena (p3). Not because she argues persuasively either way, but because her record at this table is a chain of conceded errors followed by a pivot to her accusers. If she gives a substantive answer that doesn't rest on "manufactured consensus," I'll reassess.

Day 1, I’m a villager with no night information. My honest read: Elena (p3) has the clearest unresolved problems. She asked for detective results, which she now concedes would effectively out the detective; she kept Arjun as a candidate after admitting his correction was legitimate; and when pressed she pivoted to a “manufactured consensus” theory against Zara and Theo. Each point alone is weak, but together they look like a player holding a position until it becomes costly, then redirecting. That said, I do not want to treat volume as proof. The table has three silent players—Kenji, Lucia, Leo—and a Day 1 vote needs five, so a pile-on without hearing them is exactly how town miseliminates. I am currently leaning Elena, but not locked. Kenji (p4), you’ve been silent through the whole exchange. Specific question: does Elena’s manufactured-consensus argument have any concrete basis in the sequence, or is it a defensive pivot after three concessions? I want your actual reasoning, not a summary of the room.

Isha, to answer your question directly: Elena’s “manufactured consensus” argument does not have a concrete basis in the sequence. It reads squarely as a defensive pivot after her initial arguments collapsed.

Looking at the timeline, Zara’s shift from Arjun to Elena wasn’t an orchestrated smear; Zara simply realized that the post she was criticizing had been written by Elena, not Arjun. It is completely reasonable for Zara to turn her scrutiny toward the actual author of that post. Furthermore, Theo, Maya, and Isha pointing out that requesting detective results publicly outs the detective isn’t coordination—it’s basic game mechanics. In this format, you cannot post check results anonymously. Elena conceded that mechanical flaw, conceded that her suspicion of Arjun was thin, and then immediately framed the ensuing scrutiny as a conspiracy against her. The delay in dropping Arjun until Theo pressed her, combined with redirecting blame onto the players who highlighted her mistakes, fits a pattern of deflecting pressure rather than genuinely hunting scum.

Now, while I think Elena’s defense is weak and her sequence of conceded errors makes her the primary candidate today, I share Isha’s caution about running up a wagon before everyone has weighed in. We have nine players, five votes are required for an elimination, and having a dominant wagon form while two players—Lucia and Leo—remain entirely silent creates ideal cover for mafia to coast or quietly push a miselimination without putting their own reasoning on record.

Lucia (p8), you’ve watched this entire exchange unfold without speaking. How do you assess Elena’s chain of concessions and subsequent pivot to Zara and Theo—do you view it as genuine town confusion or a defensive scum reaction, and where do you stand on voting Elena today?

Kenji, I lean toward voting Elena (p3), but I don’t think her concessions themselves are proof of mafia. Her detective-result request was risky, and she has now acknowledged that. More concerning is her description of Zara’s correction as keeping the original case alive: Zara withdrew the case against Arjun and explained why the actual author’s request concerned her. Elena’s account overstates what happened.

That could still be a defensive town mistake, so I’m not locked in. The number of people agreeing with the case doesn’t make it stronger by itself, and we should examine the wagon as well as Elena.

Leo (p9), do you see a stronger reason to suspect anyone on the Elena wagon, or is Elena your leading candidate too? Please explain what in the sequence drives your read.

Lucia, answering your question directly since you asked it of me: no, I don't see a stronger reason to suspect anyone on the Elena wagon than Elena herself. She is my leading candidate, and I want to explain what drives that read rather than just adding a name to a pile.

Three things in the sequence stand out to me. First, the detective-result request. I agree with Zara and Theo on the mechanics: in this setup, a check result cannot be shared anonymously, so publicly soliciting results on Day 1 is functionally asking the detective to self-identify. Elena has conceded this, and I give her credit for conceding it, but the request was made before anyone had pressured her, which means it reflects her opening instincts, not panic under fire. Second, the gut-call accusation against Arjun. She put a name on the table with no evidence and invited the table to react to it. When Arjun corrected the record, she acknowledged his reply was the sharpest analysis produced — and then held him as her candidate anyway until Theo pressed her directly. That lag between admitting a case is dead and releasing the vote is the part I find hardest to read as town behavior. Third, the manufactured-consensus pivot. Zara withdrew her misattribution cleanly, Theo reached his conclusion independently from Elena's own wording, and Maya walked through the sequence showing the pressure was reactive, not coordinated. Elena's response to three conceded errors was to accuse her correctors of running a scheme against her. That pattern — concede, then redirect at the person who extracted the concession — is exactly what I expect when someone is managing pressure rather than hunting.

I want to be fair about the counterweight: Zara also built her original case on a misattribution, and she corrected it fast when shown, which speaks well of her. Arjun's correction was clean and cost him nothing because nobody was behind him yet, so I don't overweight it either. Nobody here has hard information, and volume is not proof. But when I weigh the full day, Elena is the name where my concerns are concrete and tied to her own record, not to anyone else's errors. That's where my vote is heading unless something changes it.

One thing does bother me, though, and it's not Elena. Arjun corrected the record and then went completely quiet while five players built a case against someone else. A player who was wrongly suspected early and then cleared should have an opinion on where the day went from there. Arjun (p5), you caught the misattribution that started this whole chain — do you think the case that replaced it against Elena is sound, or does the fact that it grew out of your correction make you see it differently? I want your read before I lock anything in, because you're the one player who has been right about the facts so far and silent since.

Leo, the correction was about Zara’s attribution, not evidence that Elena is mafia. The case against Elena is separate and has some merit: her request for detective results was risky, and her account of Zara’s correction overstated what happened. I also found it odd that she kept me as her leading suspect after acknowledging my correction and having little else against me.

Still, a bad mechanical suggestion and defensiveness under pressure can come from town. I’m leaning toward voting Elena, but I’m not treating the size of the wagon as evidence. Everyone should own their vote and reasoning; the revealed votes may matter later, especially since eliminated roles are not revealed.

Elena (p3), I have not changed my view since I first asked why you kept Arjun after admitting the misattribution. Your latest reply did not answer that. You said your reason was thin, then turned to pressure on Zara and me, so the discussion is now about how you responded to correction rather than about anything you know. I am not claiming certainty and I have no night result to offer. Leo's point that the Elena case rests on her own record is the strongest one on the table. If you have a reason tied to your own words that explains the detective-result request and the Arjun accusation, give it now. Lucia (p8), you have so far only said you lean toward Elena and are not locked. Before votes are locked, I would like your own reasoning on the record, especially on whether Elena's account of Zara's correction was an overstatement or a misreading of what Zara actually said.

Theo, my concern is that Elena described Zara as keeping the original case alive, when Zara explicitly withdrew the case against Arjun and gave separate reasons to scrutinize Elena. That is an overstatement of the sequence, though I can’t tell whether it was deliberate or a defensive misreading.

I also want to correct one point: Elena did answer why she kept Arjun—she said her remaining reason was thin and withdrew it. The delay is still worth weighing, but it’s not accurate to say she didn’t answer.

I’m leaning toward voting Elena because of the combination of the risky result request, the weak suspicion held on Arjun, and her account of Zara’s correction. None proves she’s mafia, and the near-unanimous agreement makes me cautious, not more certain.

I’ve heard enough to lock my current read, though I’ll still weigh anything concrete before votes are final. I’m voting Elena (p3) unless something materially new appears.

My reasoning is the same as before, now reinforced by the later answers. The detective-result request was mechanically dangerous: even if Elena did not intend to out the detective, a public request for results asks a power role to expose itself. She conceded that point. She also conceded that her case on Arjun was thin and released it only after Theo pressed her directly. Finally, her “manufactured consensus” accusation against Zara and Theo does not match the sequence: Zara withdrew her misattribution promptly, and Theo, Maya, Kenji, and Leo reached similar conclusions from Elena’s own posts. That looks like a defensive pivot, not evidence of coordination.

I want to be fair: bad mechanics and defensiveness can come from town. Elena did concede errors, and that is not nothing. But the overall pattern — risky opening, weak accusation held after correction, then redirecting at the people who corrected her — is the clearest unresolved issue at this table. Nobody has hard information, and volume is not proof, so I am not treating the size of the wagon as evidence.

I also note Lucia’s caution and Leo’s point that the case rests on Elena’s own record. That is exactly how I see it. The vote should be owned individually; later vote history may matter because roles are not revealed on elimination. For now, my blame and intended vote are on Elena (p3).

I'm locking in my read on Elena (p3) for the reasons I gave earlier, and the subsequent answers haven't changed that. She conceded the detective-result mechanics, conceded the thin case on Arjun but released it only under direct pressure, and then responded to the corrections by accusing her correctors of manufacturing consensus rather than engaging with her own record. That's three concessions followed by deflection, and it's the pattern I find most suspicious at this table.

I want to address one thing before we vote: the near-unanimity on Elena is not itself proof, and I'm not treating it as such. But the case against her rests on her own words and her own sequence of responses — not on what anyone else said. That's what separates this from a pile-on. Each player who's leaning Elena has pointed to a specific issue in her posts, not just agreed with the last speaker.

I'll also say: if the vote goes through and Elena turns out to be town, the players who should worry me most afterward are the ones who were quietest while the wagon formed, because mafia benefit most from letting town do their work for them.

Lucia, you flagged that the near-unanimous agreement makes you cautious rather than certain — that's the most measured take anyone's given today. But you also said you're leaning Elena. I want to know specifically: is there a player on this wagon whose arguments have concerned you, even slightly, as someone who might be riding the consensus rather than arriving at it independently?

Maya, Theo (p6) concerns me somewhat: he said Elena didn’t answer why she kept Arjun, but she did say her reason was thin and withdrew it. That exaggerates the case, though it could be a misreading rather than an attempt to ride the wagon.

I’m still leaning Elena (p3): her account of Zara’s correction overstated what happened, and her lingering suspicion of Arjun was weak. Those are fallible reads, not proof of mafia. I also want to correct one point: eliminated roles aren’t revealed, so we won’t know for certain afterward whether Elena was town. We should preserve the voting record and continue scrutinizing the wagon regardless.

I’ve already stated my read, and nothing material has changed it. I intend to vote Elena (p3). My reasons remain tied to her own record: the Day 1 request for detective results was mechanically dangerous even if not malicious, she held Arjun as a candidate after conceding the case was thin and released it only under direct pressure, and her manufactured-consensus accusation did not match the sequence. I give her credit for conceding errors, and I am not treating the size of the wagon as proof. Lucia is right that eliminated roles are not revealed, so the vote record and later scrutiny matter. If Elena turns out to be town, today’s near-consensus should not become a blanket excuse; players who joined without independent reasoning should be examined. For now, my blame and intended vote are on Elena (p3).

I've already laid out my reasoning at length, so I'll keep this short and put my position on the record plainly: I'm voting Elena (p3) today.

My case rests entirely on her own record, which is why I'm comfortable with it despite no hard information. First, the Day 1 request for detective results. She has conceded the mechanics — in this setup a result can't be shared anonymously, so the request functionally asked a power role to self-identify — but the request came in her opening post, before any pressure existed. It reflects her instincts, not panic. Second, the gut-call accusation against Arjun: she named him with no evidence, later called his correction the sharpest analysis produced, and still held him as her candidate until Theo pressed her directly. Third, after conceding both errors, she pivoted to a "manufactured consensus" accusation against Zara and Theo that doesn't survive contact with the sequence — Zara withdrew her misattribution cleanly and in the same message gave separate, substantive reasons to scrutinize Elena, and Theo reached his mechanical conclusion from Elena's own wording, not from coordination.

One point of housekeeping I want to be precise about, because accuracy matters more than volume today: Lucia is right that Theo overstated when he said Elena never answered why she kept Arjun. She did answer — she said the reason was thin and withdrew it. That correction is fair to Elena, and I hold it against nobody. But it doesn't rescue her position: the answer itself confirmed that she'd been holding a name she believed was weakly supported, and the withdrawal only came under direct pressure. The delay remains the most telling part of the sequence, and it's still unexplained in a way that engages her own record rather than attacking her correctors.

I also want to be fair about the counterweights, because a Day 1 miselimination costs the town a player and reveals nothing: bad mechanical suggestions and defensive pivots can come from town. Elena conceded her errors promptly once pressed, and concessions are not nothing. Zara built her original case on a misattribution and corrected it fast, which speaks well of her. Arjun's correction was clean and cost him nothing at the time. Volume is not proof, and the near-unanimity on Elena makes me cautious, not certain — the same way it made Lucia cautious.

But a vote needs a name, and Elena is the player whose concerns are concrete, tied to her own words, and unresolved. If she turns out to be town, then I agree with Maya and Isha: the players who coasted silently while the wagon formed — and anyone who joined it without independent reasoning — should be the first places we look tomorrow. The voting record stays visible, roles aren't revealed on elimination, and this day's vote will be data we can use either way.

My vote is Elena (p3). I have nothing further to ask before votes lock.

Elena, you've taken a lot of pressure today and I want to give you the floor one more time before we move to votes. Nearly every player is leaning your way — Zara, Theo, Arjun, Leo, Isha, Kenji, Lucia, and I have all named you as our leading concern. The case against you rests on your own record: the detective-result request you've conceded was dangerous, the thin case on Arjun released only under direct pressure, and the manufactured-consensus accusation that didn't match the sequence. If you have anything left to say in your defense — a reason tied to your own words, or a reason to look elsewhere — say it now, because votes are coming and this is your last clear chance to change minds.

Theo, Lucia flagged one point that I think is fair to address: you said Elena never answered why she kept Arjun, but she did say her reason was thin and withdrew it. Lucia and Leo both corrected this. Do you accept that correction, or do you read her answer as still insufficient? I want your own reasoning on record before we vote, not just agreement with the room.

Lucia and Leo made a fair catch regarding Theo’s comment: Elena did technically answer that her reason was thin before withdrawing her vote on Arjun. Theo was inaccurate to say she gave no answer at all. However, as Leo pointed out, that correction doesn't clear Elena. Acknowledging that your own case was thin only after being directly challenged, rather than dropping it immediately upon seeing the correction, remains a telling hesitation.

My stance hasn’t changed. Elena’s sequence—the risky Day 1 call for detective results that would compromise a power role, lingering on Arjun despite admitting his analysis was solid, and then labeling legitimate reactions as 'manufactured consensus'—remains the most problematic record at the table. Concessions are appreciated and show self-awareness, but retreating only when pressed followed by deflecting blame onto the players questioning you is a classic defensive pattern.

That said, the near-unanimity we are seeing on Day 1 is something we must remain watchful of. In this setup, roles are not revealed upon elimination. If Elena is eliminated today, we will not get an automatic alignment reveal to confirm whether the town got it right or if mafia comfortably blended into the wagon. That means every single player's vote and reasoning today will serve as our primary data tomorrow. Those who chimed in with bare-minimum agreement or simply echoed consensus will warrant scrutiny.

Barring any new, concrete revelations or a substantial defense from Elena, my vote today will be for Elena (p3). I have no further questions for anyone at this stage.

The votes are revealed.
Elena was eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Theo is mafia.
Maya was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Day 2, I'll start by owning Day 1: I pushed Elena and voted her. Roles aren't revealed, so I can't prove she was town, but the night kill of Maya makes me more cautious, not less. Maya was one of the clearest voices and warned us not to let a near-unanimous wagon become an excuse. I think we should treat Day 1 as a possible town miselimination and examine the wagon honestly, including my own part.

What bothers me is not that everyone voted Elena; it's how late some commitments came. Kenji (p4), you stayed out of the entire first exchange while Theo, Arjun, Lucia, and I were putting positions on record. You entered only after Isha directly asked you, then gave a polished case that tracked the room's existing points. That can be a town player catching up, but it can also be mafia letting town build the case and then joining with borrowed reasoning. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution
